question.text: This corrupt New York political machine supported many Democratic politicians during the late-19th and early-20th centuries. It was depicted as a ferocious tiger by political cartoonist Thomas Nast.
question.clue: Samuel Tilden investigated a Grand Sachem ("say-chem") of this organization's corrupt namesake "ring."

swap.text: This Republican won the Presidency in 1880 over Winfield Scott Hancock. Charles Guiteau shot him and he died in July 1881.
swap.clue: This man defeated Winfield Scott Hancock to become president, and the Pendleton Civil Service Act was passed after his death.

question.leadin: This act, along with the Geary Act renewing this act for another decade, was the subject of an apologetic 2012 House resolution.
question.text: Name this discriminatory law, signed by Chester Arthur in 1882 and repealed in 1943, that banned immigration from a certain Asian nation but did not restrict immigration of other races.
question.clue: The "Driving Out" period, including the Hell's Canyon and Rock Springs Massacres, was initiated by this law.

swap.text: Bryan lost the 1896 Presidential election after being heavily outspent by this man. He was succeeded by Theodore Roosevelt after his 1901 assassination in Buffalo, New York.
swap.clue: This Ohio politician was the namesake of a high tariff repealed by the Wilson-Gorman Tariff.

question.leadin: This scandal involved the construction of the Union Pacific railroad.
question.text: Oakes Ames offered discounted shares in a namesake construction company to other congressmen in this scandal. It took place during the building of the Transcontinental Railroad.
question.clue: Peter A. Day was fired for providing ungenerous estimates in this scandal, while James Brooks was censured in the investigation following its exposure.

swap.text: During the Homestead Strike, this industrialist hired Pinkerton agents to violently occupy the Homestead Steel Works. Following the Homestead Strike, Alexander Berkman attempted to assassinate this industrialist.
swap.clue: Joseph Duveen advised this man on purchasing works like Vermeer's Officer and Laughing Girl for his Fifth Avenue mansion.

question.leadin: A monument to this ship in Central Park is topped by a gilded statue of Columbia being pulled by three hippocampi.
question.text: Name this warship which sank in Havana harbor in 1898. Although "yellow journalists" claimed it was destroyed by saboteurs, it probably fell victim to a boiler explosion.
question.clue: In 1976 Hyman Rickover published a book questioning the long-held belief about the cause of its destruction, claiming that Captain Charles Sigsbee's poor supervision of the coal bunker was the real cause.

swap.leadin: The United States government has a sinister history of massacring Native Americans.
swap.text: This incident took place on the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation in South Dakota. More than 150 men, women, and children from the Lakota Tribe were killed by James Forsyth's 7th Cavalry in this massacre.
swap.clue: This event began at Pine Ridge after one side engaged the Miniconjou and Chief Big Foot surrendered.

question.leadin: Allen G. Thurman, a 74-year-old running mate of this man, gave a bizarre speech stating, "I am not quite as well as I ought to be."
question.text: Name this Democrat who lost the 1888 election with Thurman but won four years later against the same opponent with the elder Adlai Stevenson as his running mate.
question.clue: Despite a severe drought, this man famously vetoed the Texas Seed Bill, which saw him earn the nickname "His Obstinacy."

swap.text: It called for the secretary of the treasury to purchase silver in amounts between two and four million dollars a month, negating the so-called "Crime of '73." For 15 points, identify this law, ultimately superseded by the Sherman Silver Purchase Act.
swap.clue: It replaced the "Crime of 1873" and mandated a 16-to-1 ratio after it was passed over the veto of Rutherford B. Hayes, who only complied with the minimum requirements of this law.

question.text: Dee Brown, who participated in the occupation of Alcatraz, wrote a history of the American West titled Bury My Heart at this location. Over 300 Lakota Sioux were killed in a 1890 massacre at this South Dakota location.
question.answerHtml: Wounded Knee [or Bury My Heart at Wounded Knee]
question.clue: The Big Foot Memorial Riders end their path at this place, remembering an event that began due to Black Coyote's deafness.

swap.text: During the Jack the Ripper case, London authorities questioned this man's former employee and cowboy Buck Taylor. This man's traveling Wild West show also employed the sharpshooter Annie Oakley.
swap.answerHtml: Buffalo Bill [or William Frederick Cody or Buffalo Bill Cody; reject “Wild Bill” or “Wild Bill Hickock”]
swap.clue: After killing and scalping a Cheyenne warrior named Yellow Hair at Warbonnet Creek, this man shouted, "The first scalp for Custer!"

question.text: One of the most important events of the "Erie War" was when Gould gained the support of this Tammany Hall figure by making him a member of the board of the Erie Railroad.
question.clue: In an 1871 cover of Harper's Weekly, Thomas Nast used the phrase "To the victors belong the spoils" to depict a beat-up version of this then "boss" of Tammany Hall.

swap.leadin: It passed the Sherman Antitrust and Silver Purchase Acts and raised the average tariff rate to 48.4% with the McKinley Tariff.
swap.text: Name this Congress, nicknamed for its supposed overspending.
swap.clue: This U.S. Congress whose lavish spending earned it a derisive nickname.

question.leadin: Answer the following about traditional and revivalist religions among Native Americans.
question.text: Joseph Epes Brown collected descriptions of seven Oglala religious rites from this holy man. More famously, John Neihardt collected stories, ritual descriptions, and history of the Oglala into a work wherein this man "Speaks".

swap.leadin: Name these people who ran for president of the United State with third parties in the nineteenth century.
swap.text: This inventor and owner of an epic beard manufactured the first American locomotive and ran for president with the Greenback party in 1876.
swap.clue: He obtained a patent for gelatin which he sold to Pearl Wait who invented the name Jell-O.

question.leadin: Answer some questions about anti-Mormon actions in American history.
question.text: In this 1878 case, the Supreme Court ruled that bigamy as a Mormon religious duty was not protected under the First Amendment.
question.clue: The Poland Act led to this 1878 test case, with a majority written by Chief Justice Morrison Waite. The Church allowed a man to be charged with bigamy; the Court upheld laws against polygamy against the argument that they infringed upon religious duty.

swap.text: The Toronto Women's Literary Club worked with the Ontario branch of this organization to achieve women's suffrage. Annie Turner Wittenmyer first led this originally-American organization, which had the slogan "Do Everything."
swap.clue: Matilda Carse published a predecessor to this organization's newspaper, The Union Signal.

question.text: In 1869, Smith was a delegate at the founding convention of this political party, which according to many Republicans cost James G. Blaine the 1884 election by nominating spoiler candidate John St. John. This party won a statewide office exactly once, when Sidney Johnston Catts was elected governor of Florida in 1916.
question.clue: The publication of The Hatchet and the activities of the Women's Christian Temperance Union helped generate support for this party, whose goals were briefly realized with the passage of the Volstead Act.

swap.leadin: Answer some questions about the history of birth control in the United States.
swap.text: Named for a certain postal inspector, this 1873 act made it illegal to distribute information about birth control methods through the mail.
swap.clue: Griswold overruled Connecticut's "Little" version of this 1873 Federal law, which made it illegal to distribute "obscene" information, including information on birth control, through the mail.
